readerTitle: Two late problems, one way to crack them
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (음료 유통업체의 배송 지연, 소프트웨어 회사 채용팀의 채용 지연) + 가상 적용 (제조사 재무팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 큰 문제는 한 번에 풀지 않는다. 겹치지 않고 빠짐없는 부분으로 나누면 '모든 걸 고치기'가 '바뀐 한 부분 찾기'로 바뀐다.
misconception: 큰 문제에는 큰 해결책이 필요하다. 문제를 보면 바로 해결책 아이디어부터 모아야 한다.

sources.text: 문제 분해(이슈 트리, 프로세스 분해)는 경영 컨설팅과 문제 해결 교육의 표준 기법
Minto, B. The Pyramid Principle (MECE 개념이 널리 알려진 출처로 자주 인용됨)

factChecks.note: 배송 단계 계산: 이전 2 + 6 + 3 + 5 = 16시간, 현재 2 + 26 + 3 + 5 = 36시간. 늘어난 20시간은 모두 '피킹 대기' 단계에서 발생합니다.
채용 단계 계산: 소싱 20일 + 서류 10일 + 면접 39일 + 오퍼 승인 21일 = 90일. 오퍼 승인 21일은 설명용 가정입니다.
MECE라는 용어의 기원을 Barbara Minto와 McKinsey로 돌리는 설명이 흔하지만, 카드에는 기원을 단정하지 않고 'consultants often call this MECE'라고만 적었습니다. 게시 전 표현을 한 번 더 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two late problems, one way to crack them
body: A drinks distributor hears it every week: "Your deliveries are late." Across town, the head of recruiting at a software company hears: "Hiring takes forever."
Both managers called a meeting. Both meetings ended with a list of twenty fixes and no idea which one mattered.

image.label: Two managers facing a giant tangled knot
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 창고 앞 유통업체 매니저, 오른쪽은 사무실 채용 담당자. 두 사람 앞에 각각 거대한 엉킨 실뭉치가 있고, 실뭉치에 "Late deliveries", "Slow hiring" 라벨. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Customers say deliveries are late.
body: You run a regional drinks distributor. Shops order by noon and expect delivery the next day. Lately, many orders arrive a day later than that.
Your drivers blame traffic. What do you do first?

options.text: Lease two more trucks so routes are shorter
options.feedback: It's a real fix for a road problem. But you'd pay for trucks before knowing whether the road is where the time goes.

options.text: Split the trip from order to shop into steps and time each one
options.feedback: It costs a few days of tracking. In return, you find out which step got slower instead of guessing.

options.text: Ask customers which deliveries were late
options.feedback: Useful for seeing who is affected. But it tells you which orders were late, not where inside your business the time was lost.

cards.title: The trucks were fine.
body: Order to shop used to take about **16 hours**. Now it takes 36. Every extra hour is in one step: orders sitting in the warehouse, waiting to be picked.

cards.title: Break the problem into parts
body: **Breaking a problem into parts** means splitting one big, vague problem into smaller pieces you can check one at a time.

Good parts pass two tests. They **don't overlap**, so nothing gets counted twice. And together they **cover the whole**, so nothing hides in a gap. Consultants often call this *MECE*: mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive.
"Deliveries are late" can't be fixed. "Orders wait 26 hours to be picked" can.

cards.title: Three common ways to split.
body: Most problems can be cut in one of these ways:
list: **By steps:** order, pick, load, drive. Good for anything that flows from start to finish.
**By formula:** sales = customers × orders per customer × average order. Good for numbers.
**By group:** region, product, customer type. Good when the problem may live in one corner.
cards.callout: Pick the split where you can measure each part.
cards.softwareNote: A drop in sign-ups splits the same way: visitors × share who start sign-up × share who finish. Each part points to a different team and a different fix.

cards.title: Hiring took 90 days. One step took 21.
body: The recruiting lead split hiring into its stages: finding candidates, screening, interviews, offer.

Finding took 20 days, screening 10, interviews 39. Interviews looked like the culprit, and they were long. But the surprise was the offer: **21 days** waiting for sign-off from two busy executives. Good candidates took other jobs in that gap.
A one-week approval rule fixed more than any new job board would have.

image.label: Hiring timeline split into four stages
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 4개 구간 "Finding 20 days", "Screening 10 days", "Interviews 39 days", "Offer sign-off 21 days". 마지막 구간에 모래시계 아이콘과 강조색. 실제 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Splitting can go wrong.
body: Some causes live *between* parts. The warehouse might be slow because sales started promising rush orders that jump the queue. Each step looks like its own problem, but the cause is how they interact.
Splitting can also become a hobby. Stop when a part is small enough that you know who would fix it and how you'd check.
And a bad split hides the answer. If two parts overlap, people argue about whose problem it is.

cards.title: Now it's a finance team.
body: You lead the finance team at a furniture maker. The monthly report used to be ready on day 5 of the month. Now it's day 12, and leadership is annoyed.
How do you split the problem?

options.text: By person: see which team member is slowest
options.feedback: It's easy to measure, but people share tasks, so the parts overlap. It also turns a process question into blame.

options.text: By step: collect data, check it, adjust, review, send, and time each
options.feedback: The steps don't overlap and they cover the whole month-end. You'll see where the seven extra days went.
It's a start, but the two groups overlap. A late sales file is both, so the team will argue about where it belongs.

cards.title: Don't fix the big problem. Find the part that changed.
body: Split the problem into pieces that don't overlap and cover the whole. Then measure each piece before choosing a fix.
**Try it today:** take one problem your team keeps talking about. Write its steps on a single line and put a number under each one.
